opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that there are two sources of capability gains, and they're going to keep interacting in ways that matter a lot for forecasting.

One source is just direct, in-domain training: you have some task you care about, like software engineering, you build environments for it, you do a bunch of RL, and the model gets better at that thing. That's pretty reliable. If AI companies really care about a domain and can build good environments with reasonably checkable outcomes, I expect they can push performance up a lot. The constraint is that it's labor-intensive and you need verifiable feedback, so it works best on things like coding, math, and well-specified agentic tasks.

The other source is generalization: you train on some set of narrow tasks and the model picks up something more general, like better long-horizon planning, better error correction, better research taste, that transfers to domains you never explicitly trained on. Historically, a lot of the surprising capability gains have come from this kind of transfer, especially from pretraining. With RL on narrow tasks, my sense is the transfer is real but somewhat weaker than people sometimes hope. You get some spillover, but models still tend to be noticeably better on the stuff that looks like their training distribution.

How I expect these to combine: in the near term, I think in-domain training does a lot of the heavy lifting. Companies will pick the domains that matter most economically and for AI R&D itself, especially coding and ML engineering, and grind on those. So you'd see a pretty spiky capability profile, very strong in heavily trained areas, weaker in messier, less verifiable domains.

But as models get more capable, I'd expect generalization to get better, for a couple of reasons. One is that more capable models seem to learn more abstract, reusable skills from the same amount of training. Another is that the set of narrow tasks you're training on becomes so broad and diverse that the union starts to cover a lot of what you'd want from general competence. At some point the distinction blurs: if you've trained on thousands of different kinds of agentic tasks, the "general" skill of figuring out an unfamiliar task is itself something you've trained on.

And then there's a feedback loop that I think is really important. If in-domain training makes AIs very good at AI R&D specifically, those AIs can help build more training environments, better RL setups, and so on. So even if generalization stays somewhat limited, you can use narrowly capable systems to massively scale up the in-domain training for everything else. That means the bottleneck of "humans have to build environments for each domain" might not stay a bottleneck for very long.

So my overall picture is: early on, spiky and driven by targeted training; later, broader competence through some mix of better generalization and automated scaling of in-domain training. And from a risk perspective, I think this means you shouldn't take comfort from the fact that current models are weak in some domains. That weakness may disappear fairly quickly once the AI R&D loop gets going, and it might disappear unevenly, in ways that are hard to predict ahead of time.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly predicts that capability gains will come from direct in-domain training and generalization from narrow tasks, with their balance changing as capabilities improve.

r002.rationale: It notes that in-domain training is labor-intensive and requires verifiable feedback, but does not identify scarce training data for long-horizon software engineering as a reason transfer from other tasks will be needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that right now, a lot of what we're seeing is that labs are getting really good at training AIs to do specific things they care about. Like, you train on a bunch of software engineering tasks, you get good software engineering. You train on math, you get good math. And the question is: how much of that transfers to stuff you didn't explicitly train on?

And my view is that both of these things are going to keep mattering, but the balance shifts over time. In the near term, I expect in-domain training to be doing a lot of the heavy lifting. If you want an AI that's good at, say, running ML experiments, the most reliable path is to construct a bunch of environments where it does that and train on them. The generalisation you get for free from that is real but kind of patchy — you'll see it be surprisingly good at some adjacent thing and then weirdly bad at something that seems easy.

But I think there are a couple of reasons the generalisation part becomes more important as capabilities improve. One is just that as models get smarter, they generalise further from each piece of training. We've seen this pretty consistently — bigger, more capable models need less task-specific data to get good at a new thing. So the "reach" of each training domain expands.

The other thing is that the domains the labs care most about — AI R&D, software engineering, agentic computer use — those are quite broad. Being good at the full range of AI R&D is not really a narrow task; it involves a huge amount of general problem-solving, reading papers, debugging weird stuff, forming hypotheses. So if you get really good at that through in-domain training, you've kind of incidentally gotten good at a lot of general cognition. And I think that spills over.

Where I'd push back on the most optimistic version of this is that I don't think you'll get perfectly uniform capabilities. I expect there'll be a persistent "spikiness" — the AIs will be superhuman at the things they were trained hard on and more mediocre at things that are far from that distribution. And some of the things that are hard to train on directly, like long-horizon tasks where feedback is very delayed, or tasks that require a lot of tacit knowledge that isn't written down — those might lag. That matters for stuff like forecasting when AIs can automate AI research, because some parts of that job might be easy to train and some might be the bottleneck.

So my overall picture is: in-domain training gets you most of the way on the things labs are targeting, generalisation fills in a lot of the gaps and gets better over time, and the frontier is going to look jagged for a while even as it keeps moving outward. I'd put a fair amount of weight on the view that by the time you have an AI that's actually good at the broad task of doing AI research end-to-end, it's going to be pretty general — because that task is just hard to do without being pretty general.

r001.rationale: The response says both in-domain training and generalisation will matter as capabilities improve, with generalisation becoming more important over time.

r002.rationale: It mentions long-horizon tasks as difficult to train directly, but does not identify a shortage of abundant training data for long-horizon software engineering or say those tasks will therefore require transfer from other tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think you should expect both to matter, and for them to reinforce each other. You can train a model on relatively narrow tasks where you can check whether it succeeded, and in doing so teach it skills that are useful in a much broader range of settings. Then, when you train it directly on something you care about, it’s starting with a lot of the relevant machinery already in place.

So I wouldn’t imagine a sharp distinction between ‘the model learned this in training’ and ‘the model generalised to this.’ You might train it on parts of a task, or on simpler versions, and then it generalises to putting those pieces together over a longer horizon. And you might subsequently train on those longer tasks as well.

The big uncertainty is how much direct training you need at each stage. Does getting good at a bunch of short, fairly well-specified tasks make you good at pursuing a messy objective over a week? I don’t think that follows automatically. But as models become more capable, they may need fewer examples and less specialised training to bridge that gap. So I’d expect a mixture, rather than capabilities coming entirely from either narrow-task generalisation or training on the exact thing you want.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly expects a mixture of narrow-task generalisation and direct training on the target tasks.

r002.rationale: It discusses transferring from short tasks to longer, messy objectives, but does not identify scarce training data for long-horizon software engineering as a reason for that transfer.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect both to matter, and for them to reinforce each other. You get some capability from training directly on tasks that resemble what you want the model to do, and some from generalisation from other tasks. As models become more capable, it becomes easier to generate useful training data and provide feedback on a wider range of tasks, so the scope of in-domain training expands.

For example, you might initially train a model on relatively short coding problems where you can check whether its answer works. The model might generalise from that to doing somewhat longer coding tasks. And once it can do those tasks some fraction of the time, you can potentially use that ability to produce training examples or run a training process directly on those longer tasks. So generalisation gets you into a new domain, and then training makes the capability more reliable.

The important uncertainty is how big the gaps are between those steps. If a task requires a lot of capabilities to come together before you get any useful feedback, progress could be slow. If there’s a fairly continuous sequence of tasks where you can measure success and improve, then this combination could get you quite far without requiring a single dramatic leap in generalisation.

r001.rationale: The response says both in-domain training and generalisation from other tasks will matter and reinforce each other as models become more capable.

r002.rationale: It gives an example of training on short coding problems and later longer tasks, but does not identify difficulty obtaining abundant training data for long-horizon software engineering as a reason transfer will be needed.
